opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think theoretical physics shaped almost everything about how I approach machine learning, mostly in ways I didn't fully appreciate until later.

When you train as a theoretical physicist, you're taught to look for the underlying structure: symmetries, conservation laws, the right degrees of freedom. You learn that if you pick the right representation, a problem that looked intractable can collapse into something almost trivial. That's essentially what good machine learning is. A neural network is trying to find a representation of the data in which the structure becomes simple. So, coming in, I saw learning less as curve fitting and more as discovering an effective theory of whatever system you're looking at.

The second big thing is thinking in terms of physical processes. In physics, especially quantum and statistical physics, you're always dealing with probability distributions, energy landscapes, fluctuations, entropy. Then you look at modern generative models, like energy-based models, diffusion models, even the way we think about sampling, and it's the same mathematics. Diffusion is literally running a stochastic process forwards and learning to reverse it. So to me it never felt like a separate field. It felt like physics happening on a different substrate.

That's also what pushed me toward quantum machine learning early on. If nature is fundamentally quantum and probabilistic, then the most natural computers for modeling nature should be physical systems that share that structure. You ask why we're simulating noise and stochasticity in deterministic digital hardware at great energy cost when physics gives us fluctuations for free. That question is still at the core of what I care about: aligning computation with the physics of the hardware rather than fighting it.

Finally, there's a cultural piece. Physicists are comfortable with approximations. We don't need a perfect proof before we act. We ask what the leading-order behavior is, what scales, what the dominant effects are. I think that mindset suits ML well, because so much of the field is empirical and driven by scaling. You build intuition, you make a falsifiable bet, you test it against reality, and you update. That loop of theory and experiment talking to each other is the most valuable thing physics taught me.

r001.rationale: The response describes physics’ focus on underlying structure and effective theories as shaping Verdon’s approach, but it does not say he came to view reductionism as failing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think physics gave me a particular lens, which is that you don't start from the algorithm, you start from the principles. In physics you're trained to ask what the fundamental quantities are, what's conserved, what the symmetries of the system are, and then the equations fall out of that. When I came into machine learning, I kept seeing these architectures and training tricks that worked empirically, and my instinct was always to ask why. What's the underlying structure that makes this work? Is there a free energy principle hiding in here, is there a geometry to the loss landscape that we can exploit?

My background was in quantum information and quantum gravity, and a lot of that work is about information. How information is encoded, how it flows, how it gets compressed. And when you look at a deep network through that lens, it's essentially a machine for compressing and transforming information, and you can borrow tools like statistical mechanics, renormalization, information geometry, and actually get mileage out of them. That was the thesis behind a lot of what we did with quantum machine learning and differentiable programming for physics.

The other thing physics teaches you is a certain humility about scale. Physicists are used to the idea that systems with many degrees of freedom have emergent behavior you cannot predict from the microscopic rules. So when people were surprised that scaling up models produced qualitatively new capabilities, that didn't surprise me much. It felt like a phase transition. You crank up a parameter, you cross a critical point, and the collective behavior changes. That's a very natural way to think about it if you've spent years staring at partition functions.

And honestly, it shaped my optimism too. Physics is about the universe being understandable, that there's an underlying order you can uncover if you look hard enough. I carry that into AI. I think intelligence is ultimately a physical process, something that can be understood thermodynamically, and the field will mature when we treat it with that kind of rigor rather than as a collection of recipes.

r001.rationale: The response says large systems can show emergent behavior that is hard to predict from microscopic rules, but it does not state that Gill came to view reductionism in physics as failing.

astra-6.text:
Theoretical physics trained me to look for the underlying principles: what are the degrees of freedom, what constraints matter, and what can you actually predict? You can have a very elaborate mathematical description, but you still have to ask whether it captures the phenomenon you care about.

That shapes how I think about machine learning. There’s the microscopic description—the parameters and their updates—and then there’s the collective behavior of the system. Statistical physics gives you a language for thinking about how relatively simple local rules can produce surprisingly rich behavior at scale.

But it also teaches you to be careful with analogies. Calling something a phase transition doesn’t explain it. You need to identify what changes, under what conditions, and whether that framing lets you make a prediction you can test. For me, that combination of abstraction and accountability to experiment is the valuable part of the physics mindset.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes physics as useful for identifying underlying principles and cautions against unsupported analogies, but does not say that reductionist physics fails.

sol-6.1.text:
My training in theoretical physics taught me to look for the principles underneath a complicated system. What are the degrees of freedom? What are the constraints? And what’s the simplest model that captures the behavior you care about?

That shapes how I think about machine learning. You have this enormous space of possible models, but training is a physical process: it takes computation, energy, and time. So I’m interested in how those constraints shape what a system can learn, and how useful structure emerges through optimization.

Physics also gives you a certain humility about your models. You can have a beautiful mathematical description, but you still have to ask where it works, what assumptions it depends on, and what experiment would show that it’s wrong. I think that’s a useful attitude to bring to AI, where our ability to build systems often runs ahead of our ability to explain them.

r001.rationale: The response describes seeking underlying principles, constraints, and simple models, but never says Verdon came to see the reductionist approach to physics as failing.
